So it is a positive and the numbers are going up and we want them to continue in the right direction.
Conor Garris, Chief of the National Transport Authority, thank you for joining me.
And as Conor kind of highlighted there, this data also surveyed people's thoughts on where they want to travel infrastructure invested.
Two-thirds of Dubliners want more in walking and wheeling, 55% for cycling, and just over a third want more investment in driving.
So a lot for transport bosses to mull over from this report.
But for now, Audrey, it's back to you.
Andrew, thank you very much indeed.
Andrew Loud there, out and about in Clontarf this morning.
We'll be back after the break.
You're listening to Morning Ireland.
Let's go back now to events in the Middle East and their wider impact, including on travel.
It's estimated that around 22,000 Irish people are currently in the Gulf region, which is being targeted by Iranian missiles and drone attacks.
Many of them live there, but it's estimated that around 2,000 people are there either on holidays or transiting through that area and are now stranded waiting for flights home.
We're joined in our studio now by Neil Richmond, Minister of State for International Development and the Diaspora.
Minister, good morning.
What's the latest information you have for Irish people who are stuck either in hotels or at airports in the Gulf region in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Doha and who can't get out of there right now?
How long might they be there?
Well, yesterday we saw the first flights take off from Abu Dhabi, about 15 flights, and there were some Irish people on that, and there'll be more again today.
These are primarily aimed at people who are stuck in transit.
So of those 2,000 who are visiting, about 900 are currently in transit, and the priority of the officials in the UAE is to assist them first.
Our advice is for all Irish people in the region, just over 22,000, is first and foremost to register with the embassy.
We've seen thousands of additional people register with our embassies in Abu Dhabi, in Riyadh, and to follow very closely the local advice.
Travel is extremely dangerous at the moment.
Airspace is closed.
Follow the advice of the local authorities.
and register with our officials.
Is any consideration being given by the government to chartering flights to get those people out?
Look, it would be a bit irresponsible of me to talk about speculation.
All I can say is that the government is working with European partners as per traditional routes to look at all options that are on the table.
Right.
But what does that mean?
I mean, for the people who are there and they want to know, are they to rely on their own airlines or is there help coming from the government?
Well, I think the main thing to say is airspace is closed, Justin.
Regardless of what the government do, we can't get any flights in or out to the main hub, which is the UAE.
That's where the vast majority of Irish people are.
The vast majority are transiting in.
Same with our European partners.
The first piece of information will come from commercial airlines.
As I said, Etihad were able to get a number of flights out yesterday and today focused on transit.
It's to stay in touch with your airlines.

The UAE officials have been very clear for people not to go to airports to remain is, and to credit to the UAE officials, they are covering accommodation and hotel costs for people who are stuck there.
Okay, and what's the situation with the embassy in the UAE at the moment?
Is that open or the staff operational there?
It is operational.
It's not open to the public.
There's no consular desk open, but our ambassador in Abu Dhabi only put up a video in the last hour confirming that the helplines, the emails are all open 24-7.
They've had quite a lot of traffic, as you can imagine, coming through, as has our embassy in Riyadh, but the entire operations in the Gulf is coordinated by our embassy in Abu Dhabi.
Okay.
Now, the cost of a...
Fill of oil went up by over 100 euros yesterday.

We heard from Lisa Ryan, Professor of Energy Economics, earlier in the programme, who said that that sort of jump shouldn't be happening overnight, that it should take some time before price rises on the markets actually filter down
to the consumer here.
So what's going on here?
Why has the price jumped so high?
Well, we would obviously expect prices to increase when there is huge impacts on supply, regardless of where we source our energy from.
As has been reported, the Straits of Hormuz has been closed.
The Qataris have stopped their gas production.
That will have an impact.
Now, the vast majority of Irish companies do buy in advance.
They hedge the market.
We saw that with Brent oil prices.
The increases are extremely concerning and they are perhaps in some cases quite early.
But this is an extremely difficult situation.
What happened perhaps in Ukraine when we saw prices rise over a sustained period is slightly different to what we're looking at at the moment.
When you say it's concerning and those prices have come early, does that mean you think that there's price gouging going on?
No, that's not what I said at all.
It's just concerning that we see a price of this extent.
We'd expect prices to go up absolutely when events like this happen.
We saw that before when there was previous attacks in Iran, when there was instability in the region over the last number of years.
But certainly there is very serious concern that these have come to the extent they have at the time they have.
Okay, so I mean, what do you think is going on then?
Why have they happened so quickly?
Well, I can imagine that the energy companies are looking at a situation which is extremely volatile and is...
escalated rapidly over the last four days.
Right.

But, I mean, some people in the opposition have suggested that perhaps people are being taken advantage of or that some of the oil companies are taking advantage of the situation and are upping their prices immediately when they don't have to.
Well, I heard those calls and absolutely it's up for the CRU now to make sure that they keep a watching brief on this and then analyse and they'll report to Minister O'Brien in due course.
All right.
What about energy credits?

They were ruled out by the government in the last budget, but we are now seeing the price of oil, the price of gas is going to increase and the cost of goods coming into the country is also going to increase because the cost of shipping has gone up.
Will there be help from the government for people who are struggling?
Well, I think we're only four days into this particular conflict.
The government, as always, will keep an open mind in relation to any supports that are needed to the Irish people.
There will be very serious economic impacts in relation to the Irish people based on these activities.
The government keeps an open mind on any supports that may be needed, but perhaps it's a bit premature to be getting into that right now.
All right.
Okay.
Neil Richmond, Minister of State for International Development and the Diaspora.
Thank you very much for coming to our studio this morning.
It is nine o'clock.
Thank you for listening to Justin and me this morning.
And thank you to our team, Shane Galvin, our broadcast coordinator, Ruth Kennington on sound, our editors, Brendan Fitzpatrick and Conor Barron's and series editor, John Burke.
Stay tuned for today with David McCullough up after the news at nine with Kate Carolyn.
And we'll talk to you tomorrow morning at seven.
